task_row_model.query: What are the recommended first-line oral antibiotics and typical durations for treating acute uncomplicated cystitis in non-pregnant adult women?

documents.content: Acute pyelonephritis and complicated urinary tract infections often require broader-spectrum therapy and longer courses than cystitis. Empiric IV ceftriaxone or a fluoroquinolone may be used initially for severe cases, with step-down to appropriate oral agents once clinical improvement occurs. Treatment durations are typically 7–14 days depending on severity and response. In men or patients with anatomic abnormalities, evaluation for obstruction or prostatitis is important. These scenarios differ from uncomplicated cystitis, which generally uses oral short-course regimens targeted at Escherichia coli.

documents.content: Bacterial vaginosis is treated with metronidazole or clindamycin. Oral metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for seven days or metronidazole gel intravaginally for five days are common regimens; clindamycin cream can also be used intravaginally. Treatment aims to restore the normal vaginal flora by reducing anaerobic overgrowth. Recurrence is common and patient counseling on sexual and hygiene factors may help. This condition is gynecologic rather than urinary and presents with discharge and odor rather than dysuria or frequency as primary symptoms.

documents.content: For acute uncomplicated cystitis in non-pregnant adult women, first-line oral options include nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), and fosfomycin. Nitrofurantoin (100 mg twice daily) for five days is effective. TMP-SMX (160/800 mg twice daily) for three days is appropriate when local E. coli resistance to TMP-SMX is below ~20%. Fosfomycin trometamol is given as a single 3 g dose. Fluoroquinolones are generally avoided for routine uncomplicated cystitis due to adverse effects and resistance concerns. Always assess for signs of pyelonephritis or pregnancy, which change management.

documents.content: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is the presence of bacteria in the urine without urinary symptoms and usually should not be treated except in pregnancy or before certain urologic procedures. In pregnant women, treatment reduces risk of pyelonephritis and adverse outcomes; recommended agents include beta-lactams or nitrofurantoin depending on trimester and local susceptibility. Screening is performed with urine culture. This topic is related to urinary bacteria but focuses on when not to treat rather than selection or duration of therapy for symptomatic cystitis.

documents.content: Acute otitis media in children and some adults is commonly treated with amoxicillin as first-line therapy when bacterial infection is suspected. Typical dosing is weight-based with a usual duration of 5–10 days depending on age and severity. Alternatives include amoxicillin-clavulanate for suspected beta-lactamase–producing organisms or in cases of recent amoxicillin exposure. Diagnosis is clinical based on ear pain, otoscopic findings, and systemic symptoms. This is an ENT infection and its antibiotic choices and durations differ from urinary tract infections.
